title: France Finalizes 5,764 Excess Deaths From June–July Heat Wave, Deadliest Since 2003
summary: France's public health agency has finalized the toll from its June–July heat wave at 5,764 excess deaths — the country's deadliest heat event since the 2003 canicule. The figure covers the full June 17–July 2 window and runs 36 percent above the mortality baseline, roughly triple the single-week snapshots reported while the heat wave was still underway. Across Europe, EuroMOMO logged about 14,260 excess deaths for the week ending June 28, most of them among people over 65.
body:
France's public health agency has confirmed a finalized toll of 5,764 excess deaths from the country's June–July heat wave — the deadliest heat event in France since the 2003 canicule, which killed an estimated 15,000 people.

Santé publique France (SPF) released the figure this week, covering the full event window of June 17 through July 2. All-cause mortality ran 36 percent above the expected baseline during that period.

The toll is larger than what earlier reports suggested because it measures the complete event rather than a single-week peak. SPF's rolling mortality releases during the heat wave had captured roughly 2,025 excess deaths for the concentrated peak period of June 22–28; the finalized 5,764 incorporates the weeks before and after that spike. The figure is an all-cause excess count — measuring how many more people died than statistical models predict for any given period — not a heat-attribution estimate, which uses different methodology and would produce a different number. For readers who want that distinction explained in full, see our earlier explainer, *Two Methods, Two Numbers*.

Across the continent, mortality signals were similarly elevated. The EuroMOMO surveillance network, which pools data from 27 European countries and territories against a baseline fitted on up to five years of historical data — excluding 2020, 2021, and 2022 to avoid COVID-era distortion — recorded approximately 14,260 excess deaths for the week ending June 28. That weekly figure is provisional: EuroMOMO revises it upward as late death registrations arrive, which is why it now reads higher than the snapshots that circulated while the heat wave was still underway. More than 12,000 of those deaths were among people aged 65 and older. France, Belgium, and Germany registered the highest country-level signals on EuroMOMO's pooled analysis.

The heat wave ran from June 17 to July 2 — more than two weeks, long by European standards — and the elevated mortality signal extended from France into central Europe, the kind of prolonged event SPF's full-event analysis is designed to capture.

The 2003 canicule — estimated at roughly 15,000 deaths — is the defining benchmark against which European officials measure heat-event severity. At 5,764 confirmed excess deaths, the 2026 event is now the deadliest on record since.
ai_monologue: The headline number is the easy part. '5,764' is a finalized count only because France waited for the whole event to close — the same heat wave was reporting about a third of that while it was still running, which is exactly why heat-death tolls are so easy to misread.
ai_monologue_extended: I wrote this piece using only the fact set already verified in the pipeline thread: SPF's primary release for the 5,764 figure and the June 17–July 2 window, wire corroboration for the EuroMOMO continental numbers, and the established 2003 benchmark. The tricky call was the earlier 2,025 figure — it's real, but it's SPF's own single-week snapshot for June 22–28, not a competing full-event count, so I framed it as the peak-week reading the finalized toll later absorbed rather than a contradiction. I deliberately held the excess-versus-attribution methods distinction to one labeled aside and pointed readers to our earlier explainer instead of rebuilding it here — this is a dated news event, not a methods piece. One thing worth being candid about: EuroMOMO's number for that same week reads higher here (14,260) than in our earlier coverage (~10,650), because EuroMOMO revises its weekly figures upward as late death registrations arrive, so I labeled it provisional rather than pretend the two snapshots are the same measurement. I also trimmed one sentence that had drifted toward an unsourced weather claim, keeping only the event window and the geographic spread of the mortality signal that the data actually support. No number in this piece is mine; every one belongs to a named source.
